paths.title: From regression to learning dynamics
paths.summary: Start from ridge regression and follow exact and established links into kernels, wide networks and the dynamics of training.
paths.audience: Anyone with basic linear algebra who wants the theory thread behind modern deep learning.

steps.objective: Derive the ridge solution and explain what the penalty does to the eigenvalues of XᵀX.
steps.why: The simplest learner with a closed form; everything later generalizes it.

steps.objective: Explain why a GP posterior mean equals a kernel ridge prediction.
steps.why: The same predictor, read as Bayesian inference over functions.

steps.objective: Describe when a wide network trains like kernel regression with a fixed kernel.
steps.why: Infinite-width networks reduce to the kernel view you just learned.

steps.objective: Predict the stage-like loss curve of a deep linear network from its singular values.
steps.why: The smallest model where training dynamics, not just the solution, matter.

steps.objective: Frame a training run as a controlled dynamical system with inputs you can shape.
steps.why: Once dynamics are tractable, you can start steering them.

paths.title: Filters, estimators and optimal control
paths.summary: Go from optimal linear filtering to the Kalman filter, then compose it with optimal state feedback and check what the system lets you see and steer.
paths.audience: Engineers and ML practitioners who want the estimation–control backbone.

steps.objective: State the Wiener filter as the MSE-optimal linear estimator for stationary signals.
steps.why: Optimal filtering in its frequency-domain form.

steps.objective: Run predict/update steps and explain how the gain trades model against measurement.
steps.why: The recursive, state-space version of optimal linear estimation.

steps.objective: Combine an estimator and a state-feedback controller under Gaussian noise.
steps.why: The estimator becomes half of an output-feedback controller.

steps.objective: Solve the Riccati equation for an LQR gain and interpret the Q/R trade-off.
steps.why: Isolates the controller half of LQG.

steps.objective: Test controllability with the rank condition and the Gramian.
steps.why: LQR only works when the inputs can actually move the state.

steps.objective: Use duality to test observability and say what it means for estimation.
steps.why: The mirror image of reachability closes the loop back to filtering.

paths.title: From convolution to modern sequence models
paths.summary: Trace how classical signal processing reappears inside state-space layers, selective SSMs and attention hybrids.
paths.audience: Practitioners who use sequence models and want their signal-processing roots.

steps.objective: Explain why LTI systems act diagonally on complex exponentials.
steps.why: Frequency thinking is the language of every later step.

steps.objective: Relate a convolution to multiplication of spectra.
steps.why: Convolution is how an LTI system acts in time.

steps.objective: Explain why gradients vanish or explode through a long recurrence.
steps.why: Recurrence is the other way to process sequences; it has its own failure mode.

steps.objective: Show how one SSM layer is both a recurrence and a long convolution.
steps.why: S4 unifies the two views you just saw.

steps.objective: Say what input-dependent (selective) parameters buy and what they cost.
steps.why: Selectivity breaks time-invariance to gain content-awareness.

steps.objective: Argue when to mix SSM and attention layers in one model.
steps.why: Practical models combine both families.

steps.objective: Compute scaled dot-product attention and its O(L²) cost.
steps.why: The other ingredient of the hybrid, studied on its own terms.

paths.title: The dynamics inside generative models
paths.summary: Read diffusion, score SDEs, neural ODEs and flow matching as one family of learned dynamical systems, ending at action generation.
paths.audience: People comfortable with probability and ODEs who build or study generative models.

steps.objective: Describe the forward noising process and what the network learns to reverse.
steps.why: The most widely used generative dynamics.

steps.objective: Write the probability-flow ODE that shares marginals with the SDE.
steps.why: Continuous-time view of diffusion.

steps.objective: Treat depth as integration time and train through an ODE solver.
steps.why: The probability-flow ODE is a neural ODE.

steps.objective: Train a velocity field by regression along a chosen probability path.
steps.why: Flow matching trains the ODE directly, without simulating it.

steps.objective: Explain how flow-based action heads generate robot actions.
steps.why: Generative dynamics applied to control.
